title: Investigating the role of drama-based strategies in addressing psychological trauma: a systematic review

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Investigating the role of drama-based strategies in addressing psychological trauma: a systematic review》：研究问题的原文依据。

【The aim of this review · S001-S2003-p1】The objective of this systematic review was to synthesise empirical studies examining drama-based interventions for individuals exposed to trauma. Specifically, the review aimed to describe the characteristics of drama-based interventions, the types of trauma and adversity addressed, and the pattern and range of trauma-related psychological outcomes assessed. The review also aimed to assess the quality of evidence in the field and highlight areas for future research.

【Introduction · S001-p1】Psychological trauma is a major public health concern with individual, societal, and economic consequences (Bellis et al., 2019; Magruder et al., 2017; Peterson et al., 2023). Trauma and adverse experiences have been associated with poorer overall health (Wegman & Stetler, 2009) and increased risk of a wide range of mental health conditions (McKay et al., 2021). The effects of trauma aggregate into increased demand on service utilisation, increased comorbidity, and intergenerational transmission of risk, contributing to persistent patterns of disadvantage and inequity (Bellis et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2012; Graf et al., 2021; Jonson-Reid et al., 2004). Trauma-related mental health difficulties are also associated with substantial costs, including increased healthcare expenditure (Peterson et al., 2023), reduced workforce participation (Metzler et al., 2017) and productivity losses over time (Merrill et al., 2026). Given the breadth of the individual, societal, and economic consequences, how trauma is defined becomes a central issue in shaping what is studied, measured, and ultimately addressed through intervention.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Investigating the role of drama-based strategies in addressing psychological trauma: a systematic review》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methodological quality assessment · S005-S2004-p1】Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), Version 2018 (Hong et al., 2018). The MMAT was selected because the included studies comprised qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods, and case-based designs. Appraisal criteria were operationalised in a structured Excel spreadsheet. Quality assessment was undertaken by two reviewers (EO & LG), who completed the assessment independently. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Average interrater agreement was 90.3%, details are provided in Supplementary Table 3. The full results of the MMAT appraisal for each included study are presented in Supplementary Figures 1–5 and Supplementary Table 4.

【Supplemental Material · s009-p1】Supplemental data for this article can be accessed online at https://doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2026.2739019.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Investigating the role of drama-based strategies in addressing psychological trauma: a systematic review》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · S008-p1】To our knowledge, this systematic review was the first to synthesise the existing evidence base for drama-based interventions in improving mental health symptoms in trauma-exposed populations. It identified a diverse and methodologically heterogeneous body of literature. Across psychodrama, dramatherapy, applied theatre, and other drama-based approaches, some studies reported improvements in trauma-related psychological outcomes, including post-traumatic stress symptoms, anxiety, and depression. However, the evidence base was characterised by substantial variation in intervention type, trauma context, outcome measurement, terminology, and study design, and certainty of evidence for the most commonly examined outcomes was very low.

【Conclusion · S008-p2】The findings of this review suggest that drama-based approaches may hold promise as flexible and potentially valuable non-cognitive-based therapy interventions for trauma-exposed populations across clinical, educational, and community settings, but current evidence does not permit strong conclusions regarding effectiveness or comparative benefit. Future research would benefit from more rigorous study designs, greater consistency in outcome assessment, longer follow-up, and clearer reporting of intervention content, facilitation, and implementation. Improved specification of the dramatic strategies used within programmes may also help clarify how these interventions are conceptualised and how they may contribute to trauma-related mental health care.
